summary: We are testing whether a well-engineered simulated annealing solver with penalty-aware move evaluation and prime-city scheduling can substantially beat the baseline score of 33.5 on a penalized TSP problem (problem #44). A single experimental arm will implement grid-based nearest-neighbor construction, incremental Or-opt/2-opt SA moves, and a prime-scheduling post-pass, all within a 2-second time limit.
key_points: The baseline probe (naive NN + limited SA) scored 33.5/100; this arm predicts improvement by addressing three bottlenecks: O(N²) construction cost, full-recompute move evaluation, and unexploited penalty structure (every 10th step costs 10% more unless the source city ID is prime).

The single h-main arm combines three mechanisms: (1) grid-bucketed nearest-neighbor for fast O(N√N) initial tour, (2) SA with Or-opt and bounded 2-opt moves using O(1) incremental delta evaluation that accounts for step-10 penalties, and (3) a final pass that swaps prime cities into penalty positions (indices 9, 19, 29, …) when cost-beneficial.

Confirmation: score significantly above 33.5 (target >50). Refutation: score ≤ 33.5, which would indicate either implementation bugs (diagnosable by comparing incremental vs full cost), excessive construction time leaving no SA budget, or the prime-scheduling pass undoing SA gains (diagnosable by comparing scores before/after the pass).

Key risk: N can reach 200,000 with a 2-second time limit, so the implementation must be very efficient — grid NN must be O(N√N), and SA iterations must avoid any O(N) penalty recomputation per move. The cooling rate (0.99999) and segment length cap (500 for 2-opt) are tunable if profiling shows bottlenecks.
